title: NVME Identify Controller: decode all fields
description:
This is to resolve reported issue #17282.

Since this is many changes, I suggest that commits are not squashed to single commit and the history is preserved at merge point.

This follows on merge request !2339 and completes the work on Identify Controller Response.

what it post_cb?

Alexis, thank you for your review.

So, in the previous commit, I had add_group_mask_entry() and it passed review.

There was no need for additional decoding of fields. Following the 256 byte offset, there is a repeating pattern of masks, with mask fields having a special text meaning that depends on the value.

The purpose of the callback is to allow additional decoding. You can see what callbacks do.

I do not believe there is an exiting API solution for this that will not require writing much code -- the purpose was to automate this because of so many many fields that follow this pattern.

Please also see my reply about the use of add_group_mask_entry() and add_group_mask_entry_post_cb() in the follow-up question.

it is not possible to use proto_tree_add_bitmak command family ?

Alexis, thank you for your review.

In the previous commit, I used  add_group_mask_entry() and it has passed review.

The reason I used my function, because the standard  proto_tree_add_bitmask() function would result in thrice (x4) as much code. First you need to declare each filed as int (N lines), than you need to declare the array of int * (N lines again), then describe each fields (N lines again).

What I do, I define array (1 line), then describe the fields (N lines). So, considering how much it was used, it is quite a simplification, and it has already passed the review.

As far as add_group_mask_entry_post_cb() goes, I have not found a solution with existing APIs without writing much code, and for this work, I had to decode bitmask values to text. This is what the callback does.

At this time the use of these functions is limited to NVME (static functions), I am not against of exporting them as standard APIs.

Please let me know what you think. I hope this approach will not prevent approval.

@AndersBroman, thank you for reviewing.

Looks like you are reviewing per-commit basis. This maybe confusing, since last commit moved staff around to address Alexis comments.

The ASPEC(x) is immaterial -- it is simply a shortcut to "array, array_len" construct to reduce typing and have shorter lines -- to make it easier on the eyes. I can remove it if it really bothers you.

The main purpose of using an array for bitmask decoding (instead of declaring each field as separate int) is not saving on declaration but on implementation of bitmask decoding. While bitmask decoding function exists, it requires the user to declare and array and fill it with field pointers. I have found it really awkward and resulting in 3 times more code -- field declaration, field description, and field insertion into an array.

So, what I did instead is declaring an array to start with, and having a local scope function that iterates over the array for bitmask decoding. Since there are so many bitmask decoding for Identify command, I beleive this has resulted in more readable code.

Please note that neither ASPEC nor bitmask decoding via a helper function are new constructs in this merge requests. Both existed in the previous one and you have approved it. This merge request creates no new interface -- it just adds new fields without any post_add_xxx() callbacks or post add code. I have removed all "custom" "post adds" in old and new code for Identify, since Alexis did not like it. Nothing special here.

As far as previously approved bitmask decoding function, I find it much easier to use. Perhaps we can make it an interface?

Oh so I was sloppy in my previous review...again I'm not thrilled with this way of coding. But it may be just me. BTW the bitmask coding is for better dissection performance, the value is fetched only once for all bits in the field rather than optimum way of writing.
I'm done here for now.

@AndersBroman, thank you for your review, and a warning that you are taking a break....

I have looked again at proto_item_add_bitmask_tree() and proto_tree_add_bitmask(). I doubt that your assertion about performance is true... There are two cache misses there hurting performance -- a) for filling of array of pointers, b) for iterating over array and fetching field values from their pointers. The rest of the code iterates over the fields (as mine code does) and adds one field after another. It is true that it uses a parsed value -- proto_tree_add_uint_xxx() instead of  proto_tree_add_item(), but I doubt that it is going to matter since entire field already cached. What does matter though, that many branching points in  proto_item_add_bitmask_tree() will hurt performance. I can benchmark both versions for my use case -- I am sure that my version will be significantly faster.

I do not think the puprpose of proto_item_add_bitmask_tree() was performance. If it were, then we would have to use per-type versions to void branching, and use array of values for fields and not array of pointers. Looks like the focus here was a simpler interface (coding). Unfortunately, creation of sane and convenient interfaces is the art that many miss.

I am a big fan of convenient interfaces that results in easy use of interface and simpler coding. This saves bugs in real-world use...

Do we have a verdict here? I really do not think my pattern is so different from proto_tree_add_bitmask() -- it results in identical code flow, with exception that I do not need to declare array on the stack and fill it -- I have an array to start with. I seriously doubt there is a performance issue here -- on the opposite, it shall be faster. By the way, using it my way most definitely will avoid ordering mistakes -- it is not possible to display fields in in-correct order by filling array incorrectly.

Just out of curiosity, I have compared the CPU utilization approaches on the largest bitmask (16 entries).

Code (quick, only Unix):
```
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <time.h>

static inline uint64_t get_uptime_ns(void)
{
    struct timespec spec_tv;
    uint64_t res;
    clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &spec_tv);
    res = spec_tv.tv_sec;
    res *= 1000000000;
    res += spec_tv.tv_nsec;
    return res;
}

#define timed_call_stub(__cb__, arg0, args...) \
    uint64_t __nsecs__; \
    uint64_t __in__, __out__; \
    __in__ = get_uptime_ns(); \
    __cb__(arg0, ##args); \
    __out__ = get_uptime_ns(); \
    __nsecs__ = __out__ - __in__

#define timed_call(__cb__, arg0, args...) \
do { \
    timed_call_stub(__cb__, arg0, ##args); \
    fprintf(stderr, "timed call: " #__cb__ " took %lu ns\n", __nsecs__); \
} while(0)

void decode_rrls(proto_tree *tree, tvbuff_t *tvb)
{
    int *array[] = {&hf_nvme_identify_ctrl_rrls[1], &hf_nvme_identify_ctrl_rrls[2], &hf_nvme_identify_ctrl_rrls[3],

                    &hf_nvme_identify_ctrl_rrls[13], &hf_nvme_identify_ctrl_rrls[14], &hf_nvme_identify_ctrl_rrls[15],
                    &hf_nvme_identify_ctrl_rrls[16], NULL
    };
    proto_tree_add_bitmask(tree, tvb, 100, hf_nvme_identify_ctrl_rrls[0], ett_data, array, ENC_LITTLE_ENDIAN);
}
```

Alos, using proto_tree_add_bitmask(), if I go far ahead (frames count), and then back to the Identify frame, I can get sporadic increased times of 20-30 us. I can only explain that by uncaching the pointers value. I have not seen this with my approach, but I have not included it in the results, since I could not reproduce it reliably.

I believe I have demonstrated that my approach wins in terms of CPU, though it would bot be my preference for selecting it. I have chosen it for two reasons: 1. do not fill array for each bitmask. 2. avoid errors of adding fields in incorrect order.
